q: What are the assumptions of linear regression?
a: Linearity in parameters, independent errors, homoscedasticity (constant error variance), normally distributed errors (needed for p-values and confidence intervals, not for the point estimates), and no severe multicollinearity. Check with residual vs fitted plots, Q-Q plot, Durbin-Watson and VIF.

q: What is the difference between R² and adjusted R²?
a: R² = share of variance explained; it never decreases when you add a feature, even a random one (in-sample). Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − p − 1) penalises extra features and only rises if the new feature improves the fit more than chance would.
On training data with an intercept, no. On test data, yes: if the model predicts worse than simply using the mean of y, SS_res > SS_tot and R² < 0. Also possible when fitting without an intercept.

q: What happens with multicollinearity, and how do you detect and fix it?
a: Coefficients become unstable, with large standard errors and sometimes flipped signs, although predictions may still be fine. Detect with a correlation matrix or VIF (> 5–10). Fix by dropping or combining features, Ridge regression, or PCA.

q: Is polynomial regression a linear model?
a: Yes. "Linear" means linear in the parameters, not the features. \(y = w_0 + w_1x + w_2x^2\) is still solved with ordinary least squares on the features x and x².

q: Why do we minimise squared error rather than absolute error?
a: Squared error is smooth and differentiable, gives a closed-form solution, and corresponds to maximum likelihood when errors are Gaussian. It also penalises large errors more. The downside is outlier sensitivity; absolute error (median regression) or Huber loss are more robust.

q: Normal equation vs gradient descent: when to use which?
a: Normal equation \((X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\): exact, no learning rate, but costs \(O(p^3)\) for the inverse and needs all data in memory. Fine up to a few thousand features. Gradient descent (or SGD): scales to huge n and p, works with streaming data, needs a learning rate and scaled features.

q: What if you have more features than rows (p > n)?
a: \(X^\top X\) is singular, so OLS has infinitely many solutions and will fit training data perfectly. Use regularisation (Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net), dimensionality reduction, or feature selection.

q: What is the dummy variable trap?
a: If you one-hot encode all K levels and include an intercept, the K columns sum to the intercept column: perfect multicollinearity, so \(X^\top X\) is not invertible. Drop one level (it becomes the reference). Regularised models and trees don't need this.

q: How do you interpret a coefficient when y is log-transformed?
a: For \(\log y = \dots + w x\), a one-unit increase in x changes y by about \(100\,w\)% (exactly \(100(e^{w}-1)\)%). In a log-log model, w is an elasticity: 1% change in x → w% change in y.

q: Heteroscedasticity: does it bias the coefficients?
a: No, OLS coefficients stay unbiased, but their standard errors are wrong, so p-values and confidence intervals are unreliable. Fix with robust (White/HC) standard errors, weighted least squares, or a log transform of y.

q: Correlation vs causation: can you say a coefficient is the causal effect?
a: Only under strong assumptions (no omitted confounders, no reverse causality). Otherwise it is an association conditional on the other features. For causal effects use experiments (A/B tests) or causal methods (difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, propensity matching, uplift models).
